The Dark Knight wants to know: are some lives with more than other lives? According to an individual, yes; on a population level, no. I do find I get more of this movie on each rewatch. The dialogue is so quick and we are ultimately tasked with with following city politics. Reminded me of The Wire , in that way. This time around, I found the last ~30 minutes to be a bit sloppy, particularly Batman running around the building with “sonar” vision being directed by Lucius. However, the run time really does fly by. An aside: at a bar before the movie, the 22-year old bartender said to us, “Oh? Heath Ledger died?” And we said yes queen…in 2008. I don’t often feel old, but that indeed made me feel old.

This is everyone’s favorite adaptation of Batman? Are we watching the same movie? In celebration of the Lego Batman’s dlc release tomorrow I decided that this movie needed a rewatch. First, Heath Ledger is phenomenal. Outside of J.K. Simmons in Whiplash , Heath Ledger is probably my favorite performance ever. Bale has never completely convinced me as either Bruce Wayne or Batman. And the voice sucks!!!! Pattinson’s Bruce feels like someone consumed by being Batman while Bale’s Bruce often feels like he is simply operating within Nolan’s crime story. I heavily prefer Reeves’ dark and gothic Gotham to Nolan’s much brighter Chicago setting city. There are times when TDK feels less like a Batman movie and more like an extremely well-made crime thriller that happens to have Batman in it. How can I even call this a Batman movie when Joker commands most of the screen time? Batman feels strangely disconnected from being the “world’s greatest detective”. The fingerprint reconstruction scene is supposed to demonstrate his detective abilities, but it mostly amounts to technology doing the detective work for him rather than Batman being this great detective with supreme intelligence. The same goes for his equipment. Reeves makes Bruce’s obsessive commitment to building and modifying his own gear part of his characterization whereas Nolan’s Batman has Lucius Fox seemingly hand him whatever the plot requires. And what exactly is this sorry ass excuse for this brightly lit Batcave? Some of the movie’s logic also loses me. The entire Hong Kong sequence feels excessive and out of place. Batman supposedly doesn’t kill despite blowing things up everywhere he goes. Rachel falls off a skyscraper and walks away seemingly unharmed. More importantly, the Joker’s plans work with almost supernatural precision. Every person seems to react exactly as he anticipates, every piece falls into place, and almost nothing meaningfully disrupts his schemes. Ledger is so magnetic that he makes you want to overlook it but it’s hard. I also understand the thematic purpose of the Joker having no conventional motive. He represents chaos and wants to prove that civilized people can be pushed into abandoning their morals. But committing chaos for the sake of it has never been as interesting to me as it apparently is to everyone else. The character motivation feels deliberately vague in a way that doesn’t completely work for me. Still, I don’t want my complaints to make it sound like I think this is a bad movie. Far from it. Nolan knows how to construct a great movie, and there are some incredible sequences here. The truck flip and the hospital blowing up remain ridiculously cool. I also wonder how much of the Batman debate is generational. A lot of millennials grew up with Bale as the Batman, while Gen Z got Pattinson at a formative age. Maybe I’m simply more drawn to what Reeves thinks Batman should be: this lonely gothic loser detective boy that’s inseparable from Gotham itself. I just think Reeves’ The Batman runs laps around this iteration of Batman. The Dark Knight is a good movie but I’m just not convinced it’s my version of a great Batman movie. B+ish

What a sequel. Firstly the theme of fear doesn’t leave from the first movie, it prolongs and evolves into selfishness, revenge and mistrust. The Joker plays such an important role not in and of himself but as a symbol of insanity and the power of brainwashing and manipulation which was awesome. This is said so many times by everyone who has seen this movie, but holy shit Heath Ledger couldn’t have made this character feel more alive. I loved Batman’s evolution to the path of what must be done, becoming a criminal to prolong Harvey Dent’s (Pre two face) ideologies and social prowess, the telephone tracker he used with Lucius Fox holding no real power over it, and his overall selflessness. This film didn’t just feel like a superhero movie, but felt more like a proper movie that was written to explore more than just bad guy vs good guy cliches. I need to watch this film again as I had 2 break in between but I still think it was incredible. A few continuity errors at the end that threw me off but not anything major, heavy breathing and difference in voice of Batman was also slightly humorous but not in the way I think it was trying to be perceived. P.S if I come back and read these reviews in 3 months time and I haven’t played the Batman games then I will be disappointed in myself.

AMAZING MOVIE. Heath Ledger, Aaron Eckhart, Christian Bale and more put up an amazing performance in this movie. Heath Ledger as the Joker is undoubtedly one of the best portrayals of a villain. Heath is thee JOKER himself. His dialogue, his shift in tone, facial expressions, his mannerisms and more are exactly who you would imagine the Joker to be. 10/10 performance by Heath and he made this movie what it is. Aaron Eckhart as Harvey Dent was phenomenal and you can really feel how much of a tremendous symbol of hope he was for everyone in Gotham. Christian Bale’s Batman this movie was a HUGEEE step up from the first one. We see him alot more in the suit, and we see the sacrifice plays he has to make in order to be the dark knight of Gotham. The moral debates, the action sequences, the cinematography, the dialogue, the plot, the character developments and more are what make this movie arguably one of if not thee best superhero movie of all time. It should serve as a blueprint. Con, at times I do feel like it did jump around a little bit. Another con is how underdeveloped Rachel feels. In both the movies it’s a little hard to connect with Rachel, and understand the way Bruce or Harvey feel. This isn’t really a con but the performances put up by Aaron and Heath at times overshadow Christian Bale’s performance. However that’s just how good the villains were in this movie. Once again, Heath Ledger as joker is just unbelievable. This performance he put up is inspiring and you really FEEL the tension he brings. For superhero movie standards this is a 4.5/5

What an amazing movie.🥵 In terms of technical aspects, this Nolan movie was Brutal, and it was like reading a Batman comic all along: plot, characters, scenes... just spechless. In fact, It reminded me to the comic "Batman: White Knight" , in spanish: "Batman: El caballero blanco" And I think it aged like fine whine, due to Nolan's obsession to limit the CGI effects and to prefer a more practical solutions. But I have to say that Batman costume sometimes seems like a Cosplay, with Christian Bale's head big like a ballon in a tiny mask Jajajajaj. And also the motorbike that Batman uses sometimes looked like cheap plastic. Yes, I mean the weapons that were places in front of the motorbike, that rattle like a motherfucker. ****Spoilers ahead**** I saw it some years ago and I didn't understand anything. This time was different. First of all, the Joker. What a f*cking villain!!! How he manipulates everyone in the movie, even Harvey, the Gotham's "White Knight", who was the hope to stop organized crime and became Batman existence needless. The Joker always was two or three steps ahead. And Heath Ledger ... I know Joaquín Phoenix was deeply inspired by Jared Leto when he played Joker in the "Joker" movie, from 2019. Batman was fine, Fox was the best, and Harvey more of the same. I liked how Harvey's character was always the only hope to make Gotham a city criminal free. And how Joker  knew that, and started to miscontrue and manipulate all the tale to screw it up. Also, the Batman rule of "no kill" bringing it to the limit, and in the finale, with the Ferris, to demostrate that people is bad and how they will kill others for their own survival. But, like Batman said, people was still good hearted and empathic, and didn't blow everyones up. On the other hand, back in the days I didn't like much the fights, and today I kinda think the same, but this time I was able to better appreciate what was happening in each scene. The scene when Alfred burns Rachel's letter.... Nolan, what a fucker you are... In real life I think it's a bad choice, because Rachel's final wish to Bruce, was let him know that other man has reached her heart. And surely that would have helped Bruce get over his loss faster. But that resonates with the ending of Nolan's film, as it mirrors the moment when Gordon and Batman decide to cover up Harvey's final crimes as "Two-Faces" in order to keep hope alive in people's hearts and portray him as a hero who didn't live to see a new day. It all sounds very poetic, but it echoes what Harvey himself said at the beginning—and Batman at the end: "You either die a hero, or you live long enough to become a villain." This sentece, apart of being so realistic, is incredible and one of the best senteces in cinema. But, as a final message, I didn't like that sometimes you have to lie to keep people happy. I think telling the truth is always better, and more than nothing: Is true. In resume: almost a perfect movie about superheroes, but I still prefer Sam Raimi Trilogy because of their action, well aged effects, hearted plot, and my nostalgia (I saw them as a kid). This maybe is a 9 or 9'5, but some fights and some practical effects, like Batman costume, and maybe some plot holes, not became It for me a 10/10. In the end, Batman escapes, but Gordon hadn't yet told the police to pursue him. Although, thinking about it now, maybe the director was trying to tell us that that was going to happen to him from then on. I don't know, but it was weird. To sum up finally, this shit was good . 9/10. "Porque no es un héroe. Es un Caballero Oscuro" 🦇🚬🍿

Watched this at a packed out screening in 35mm… this movie has never hit so hard. Unfathomably good character work—some of the best ever written. What makes this a masterpiece, among many other things, is its commitment to pitting these opposing ideologies against each other with such force. Every scene is working to elevate the central conflict: hope vs. cynicism, chaos vs, order, cruelty vs. hope. It’s brutally honest about tragedy, but more than anything, a resounding appeal to have faith in people. Felt like I was watching this for the first time again. You thought we could be decent men in an indecent time. You may lose your faith in me, but don’t lose your faith in people.

It’s really interesting how for a movie all marketed and focusing around the Joker and the pandaemonium he causes, how the central ideas all revolve around duality. At it’s core it’s all about honing in on characters wants vs their needs. Selfish desires vs responsibilities. Batman desperately wants Rachel, to settle down and have a happy life. But is obviously responsible to keeping up his mantle as Batman. By letting Harvey be Gothams white night Batman in his hopes and dreams is no longer needed. But unlike Bruce, Harvey can be Gotham’s savior and Rachel. Or so he thinks. Harvey thinks he can have his cake and eat it too. Using the law to put all the cities criminals behind bars, but attempting to do so under an inherently corrupt and decaying system makes him vulnerable to the same dangers that Batman himself is. You can do this with every character and it just keeps looping around like a snake eating its own tail. While understanding want vs need is such a basic attribute to solid screenplays and character work, this film has that idea built into its thematic DNA. As a result it’s rock solid and still as absolutely perfect as it’s hyped up to be.
